content: The concurrent use of bedaquiline and delamanid for a six-month treatment period is being compared to a regimen where these two drugs are not used together for the same duration. The outcomes being evaluated include the successful completion of treatment (or lack thereof), bacteriological cure by the end of treatment, adherence to treatment (or interruptions due to non-adherence), treatment failure or relapse, survival (or death), adverse events associated with anti-tuberculosis medications, and the development or amplification of drug resistance. Specific questions being addressed include: 1. In the EndTB dataset, are treatment outcomes improved with the concurrent use of bedaquiline (BDQ) and delamanid (DLM) compared to the use of BDQ without DLM, in addition to other components of an adequate multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) regimen? 2. In the combined IPD-2019 and EndTB datasets, are treatment outcomes improved with the concurrent use of BDQ and DLM compared to other treatment options? Challenges in this analysis include variability in the use of DLM across different sites in the EndTB study. DLM may have been initiated at the start of therapy, introduced later, or used as salvage therapy. If added later, its use may have been influenced by local or individual preferences, protocols, or the patient’s response to therapy up to that point. Therefore, the analysis will begin with a detailed descriptive evaluation, comparing patients who received DLM to those who did not, within the EndTB dataset. Similar descriptive analyses will be conducted for the IPD-2019 dataset, which likely faces similar challenges. This will include an assessment of the timing of DLM initiation and the duration of its use. The study population and data sources for this analysis include the IPD-2019 dataset. In 2018, an individual patient data (IPD) dataset was compiled from 53 datasets across 40 countries/regions, containing records for 13,000 MDR-TB patients. This IPD-2018 dataset was analyzed to address several PICO questions developed by a WHO MDR-TB guidelines development group (GdG). These guidelines have since been published. The IPD-2018 dataset itself was based on an earlier IPD dataset assembled in 2016–2017 to address questions from a GdG of the CDC/ATS/IDSA/ERS. While these guidelines have not yet been published, the analyses informing them were published in The Lancet in September 2018. The IPD-2019 dataset represents an update of the IPD-2018 dataset. Additional data from a national surveillance program in South Africa is anticipated, and previous records of patients treated in the EndTB observational study included in the IPD-2018 dataset will be removed to avoid duplication and overlap with the new EndTB dataset. Two other datasets may also be added in response to a public call for data contributions. The EndTB dataset includes 1,094 MDR-TB patients treated with regimens containing bedaquiline and/or delamanid between April 1, 2015, and March 31, 2017. These patients were followed as part of an observational study conducted by three NGOs: Partners in Health (PIH), Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), and Interactive Research and Development (IRD). The approach for this analysis will mirror that of PICO 3, focusing on the same outcomes. The distribution of treatment duration for patients receiving BDQ and DLM will be observed to define a six-month duration. Descriptive analyses will be conducted for the intervention population receiving BDQ and DLM for six months, and statistical analyses will compare this group to comparator populations, including: 1. Patients who received only BDQ. 2. Patients who received only DLM. 3. Patients who received BDQ and DLM for less than six months. 4. Patients who received BDQ and DLM for more than six months. Analyses will be limited to the EndTB dataset, as it contains sufficient detail to control for numerous time-varying confounders that may influence which patients fall into the intervention group or one of the four comparator groups. Limitations of this analysis include challenges similar to those in PICO 3, with fewer patients treated in the IPD-2019 or EndTB datasets, limiting the ability to match on key confounding covariates and reducing statistical power to detect small benefits or harms. Additionally, there may be greater selection biases and immortal time bias affecting estimates of DLM’s effect on outcomes.
